segment_text: maybe I am missing the point and I am happy to be corrected, but the arguments made in this submission or the observations obtained are already well-known empirically, especially in the case of zero-shot and few-shot learning with very large pre-trained transformer models.
pred_justification: The paper's core contribution is a controlled study on simplified PCFG/HMM/OPT-generated datasets showing pre-training loss does not fully explain downstream performance and that flatness correlates with it, with theoretical proofs of implicit bias via SGD—this is not the well-known zero-shot/few-shot large-model phenomenon the reviewer vaguely gestures at. The segment provides no citation or specific reference to what "already well-known" finding overlaps with the paper's actual claims about implicit bias and flatness.

segment_text: In addition, the theorems mentioned in the submission don't seem necessary, or, in any case, support the arguments or the observations.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly connects Theorem 3.3 to the empirical flatness trend ("following the prediction of Theorem 3.3", Section 4/Figure 3) and Theorem 5.1 formally proves that the flattest solution in the synthetic Dyck setting is the transferable one, directly supporting the paper's central claims, so the reviewer's assertion that the theorems are unnecessary or don't support the observations overlooks these explicit connections.

segment_text: Given this challenge, I am not entirely sure whether this GPT-2 fine-tuning or GPT3 generation is very novel for this paper to be accepted as ICLR paper.
pred_justification: The paper's contribution is the GAL self-training framework using synthetic data from unconditional generative models (with theoretical analysis via empirical/vicinal risk minimization and broad experiments on text, tabular, KD, and few-shot tasks), not merely "GPT-2 fine-tuning or GPT-3 generation" as a novelty claim; GPT-2 fine-tuning is only the data-generation mechanism, and GPT-3 is mentioned only as future work (line 57).

segment_text: Considering a GPT-2 is incorporated additional for data generation, it is not surprising to observe improvements.
pred_justification: Using a fine-tuned GPT-2 for data generation IS the paper's core proposed method (GAL), not a hidden confound; the authors extensively ablate this (e.g. Section F/Table F.1, Table 6) and explicitly attribute gains to the synthetic data. Dismissing the improvement as "not surprising" because GPT-2 is used trivializes the very contribution being evaluated.

segment_text: This can only show that using additional LM for data augmentation is useful and such a claim is provided in many existing papers.
pred_justification: The paper's contribution is not merely "using additional LM for data augmentation is useful" — it presents a theoretical grounding via empirical/vicinal risk minimization (Section 4.2) explaining why unconditional (not class-conditional) generative models work, systematically ablates GAL's components (Section 5.4), and demonstrates the framework across KD, self-training, and few-shot learning on both NLP and tabular tasks, which goes beyond prior data-augmentation claims.

segment_text: The motivation is clear but corresponding empirical analysis are missing.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly states in Section 5 that "extensive experiments on several weakly supervised datasets" were conducted, and results directly support the motivating hypothesis ("These results support our initial hypothesis of LFs' importance in applying cross-validation techniques for weak supervision"), so the claim that empirical analysis for the motivation is missing is unsupported and does not specify what analysis is actually absent.

segment_text: The method is based on an intuition that a “mismatch between predictions of a model and labels can indicate candidates of noise specific to all held out labeling functions.” This intuition needs stronger support and explanation beyond a few examples mentioned in Figure 1.
pred_justification: The paper grounds this intuition in the well-established principle of k-fold cross-validation for noise detection (citing Northcutt et al. 2021; Wang et al. 2019c), explains it theoretically in the Introduction (page/section 1), and validates it with extensive experiments across six datasets and multiple baselines (Tables 1-2), not merely "a few examples mentioned in Figure 1" which only illustrates noisy label examples, not the paper's sole support for the method.

segment_text: From the Table 2 results, which use the WRENCH benchmark implementations (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2109.11377.pdf) the reported performance numbers don't seem to match what was reported in the original WRENCH paper.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly states baselines use "the Wrench implementations (Zhang et al., 2021)" (line 57) and follows Wrench's encoding/parameter conventions (line 85), so a discrepancy check against the original WRENCH paper's reported numbers is a specific, verifiable, in-scope comparison rather than a vague or out-of-scope critique; however, the paper also notes it used random hyperparameter search (not grid search) and different train/eval settings, which could legitimately explain some numeric differences, so full reliability can't be confirmed without independently checking WRENCH's published table.

segment_text: I have some concerns on the reported numbers (replicating WRENCH and reported above)
pred_justification: The segment is merely an introductory phrase ("I have some concerns on the reported numbers (replicating WRENCH and reported above)") that states a concern exists without specifying what is wrong with the numbers; the paper does state in Sec 5 that "For the baselines, we used the Wrench implementations (Zhang et al., 2021)," but without the substantive critique that presumably follows this lead-in, the segment itself provides no specific, checkable claim against the paper text.

segment_text: There are virtues to a simple method for improving performance, say an deep empirical dive into k-fold estimation when designing labeling functions, but this manuscript doesn't provide enough details to be very illuminating.
pred_justification: The paper's entire contribution is a detailed k-fold cross-validation-based algorithm (ULF/DeepULF) for denoising weak supervision labels, described with explicit methodology, so claiming the manuscript "doesn't provide enough details" about this k-fold approach is an unsubstantiated, vague critique not grounded in the paper's actual content.

segment_text: As estimating T* and Y* is the core of ULF, the paper should have some analyses on whether T* and Y* are estimated more correctly after each iteration.
pred_justification: The paper describes the iterative T*/Y* re-estimation in Algorithm 1 and reports only final aggregate performance (Tables 1-2) and iteration counts for early stopping (Sec. "Feature-based ULF": stops if labels unchanged after three iterations), but does not present analysis tracking the correctness of T* or Y* across iterations against ground truth, so the reviewer's specific request is grounded in an actual omission.

segment_text: more analyses are needed to understand the quality of T* and Y*.
pred_justification: The paper indeed never reports intrinsic evaluation of T* or Y* quality (e.g., accuracy of T* vs. true LF-class mapping, or Y* label accuracy vs. gold labels), only downstream classifier accuracy (Tables 1-2), so the underlying gap is real; however the segment itself is vague, not specifying what analyses ("more analyses") would be needed.

segment_text: Clarity: the paper is quite difficult to read as the cross-validation-based confidence estimation description is quite dense.
pred_justification: Section 3.3-3.4 is genuinely dense: it packs multiple fold-splitting variants, threshold-based confidence formulas, and a re-estimation equation (Eq. 5-7) into compact notation with terse prose, supporting a fair readability critique, though "clarity" judgments are inherently subjective.

segment_text: The paper suffers from clarity issues.
pred_justification: The segment gives no specifics about what is unclear; the paper text (methods, tables, case-study section with detailed examples like "Sample 1... Sample 2...") is written in a fairly standard, detailed style, so an unsubstantiated "clarity issues" claim with no pointer to a confusing passage is a vague/generic critique.

segment_text: For example, the feature-based and deep ULF methods need more methods elaboration and details
pred_justification: The paper provides detailed algorithmic descriptions (Section 3, Algorithms 1-3, Eqs. 1-7) and an extensive Appendix D with implementation details, hyperparameter search spaces, and training setups for both feature-based ULF and DeepULF; the segment does not specify what elaboration is missing, making it a vague, unsubstantiated critique.

segment_text: It's hard to draw any strong insights from the experiments as presented.
pred_justification: The paper presents extensive experiments across six datasets with standard errors over ten trials (Table 1), detailed results in Table 2, ablations in the appendix, and a qualitative case study (Fig. 4) explaining specific mechanisms; the segment gives no specific reason why insights can't be drawn, making it an unsubstantiated, generic critique.

segment_text: Within the paper, this is left very vague.
pred_justification: The segment simply asserts something is "left very vague" without specifying what concept, method, or claim is being referenced, matching the Vague Critique pattern where the reviewer fails to identify the missing/unclear component; without a specific referent, this criticism cannot be checked against the paper's actual content (e.g., the detailed methodology in Sections on P3 language and learner families) and offers no actionable specificity.

segment_text: The main concern I have with this paper is that I am not sure how the concept of witness set as used in this paper is learnable by a machine or a human.
pred_justification: The paper gives a precise formal definition of witness sets and teaching size (following Telle et al. 2019) and describes a concrete experimental protocol (WS, WS+AS I, WS+AS I+AS II phases) for testing exactly how learnable these witness sets are by GPT, program induction systems, and humans, directly addressing the reviewer's stated concern.

segment_text: Looking at the examples in Table 1, there are numerous ways of generalizing the first WS, some of them of similar simplicity (e.g., copy the first character, copy the last character, copy the entire sequence, etc.).
pred_justification: Table 1 (with actual example content) isn't visible in the extracted text, but the paper's own framework (Sec 3) explicitly builds in a total order over programs by length with lexicographic tie-breaking specifically because multiple programs/concepts of similar simplicity can be consistent with the same small witness set — this is a real and acknowledged tension in the teaching-size approach, so the reviewer's point about ambiguity of the minimal WS is plausible, though it isn't fully verifiable without seeing the specific Table 1 examples referenced.

segment_text: Moreover, it is impossible to learn C4 from the single WS example.
pred_justification: The paper's example table shows concept c4's witness set (WS) consists of a single example {('0','011')} (line 225), and the paper itself acknowledges WS is "the case with very few examples" where performance is poorest (line 292), supporting the reviewer's concern that learning from a single WS example is difficult; this is a paper-specific, textually grounded observation rather than a misunderstanding, though "impossible" may be a slight overstatement.

segment_text: Because there was a lack of analysis of the rule type, focusing only on an abstract idea of simplicity based on a particular method of compression, I found this unconvincing as a study of a general simplicity prior.
pred_justification: The paper defines simplicity solely via program length in the P3 language (Section 3, "simplicity, which can be formally deﬁned as the size of the concepts... Let l(p) be the length in bits of a program p in L") and bins concepts only by number of operators (VL-C/L-C/H-C/VH-C), never analyzing how the type of algorithmic rule (e.g., iterative vs. conditional, or 'reverse' vs arithmetic) independently affects results. The authors themselves acknowledge this limitation when discussing the VH-C anomaly ("if one concept is 'reverse' and we have the reverse function in the background knowledge... As P3 does not have background knowledge, the concept is categorised as complex... even if GPT-3 and Louise... can solve it"), which supports the reviewer's point that the compression/complexity metric used is representation-specific rather than a general, rule-type-aware simplicity prior.

segment_text: This makes me unsure of the interpretation of the results in this paper.
pred_justification: The segment gives no specific reason for the reviewer's uncertainty about interpretation—no reference to a particular figure, metric, or claim in the paper (e.g., Sections 5/6 discuss learning curves, characteristic curves, and error disagreement in reasonable detail with explicit caveats like the VH-C misalignment explanation), so the critique cannot be checked against any concrete textual claim and reads as an unsupported generic statement.

segment_text: Can you provide a formal definition of a concept?
pred_justification: The segment asks for "a formal definition of a concept" without specifying which concept, term, or paper passage is unclear, making it too generic and unactionable to verify against any specific content in the paper.

segment_text: The authors discuss it rather informally in the intro and related work (e.g., the concept of an odd number), but then treat it as a function in #150 and onwards.
pred_justification: The paper does introduce "odd number" informally in the intro (line 47-48) without formal definition, then at line 146-154 formally defines concepts as functions mapping inputs to outputs (starting near line 150), matching the reviewer's specific and verifiable observation.

segment_text: The number of programs is low (only 8), which the authors justify as balancing between obtaining robust results and limiting the human effort needed.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly states it uses only 8 concepts/programs and justifies this as "a trade-off for a minimally robust evaluation and the limitations of conducting the experiments with humans" (lines 218-220), matching the reviewer's characterization exactly.

segment_text: Furthermore, even if we were satisfied with just accuracy, why not get the accuracy on a much larger sample size than 15 per concept (at least for the non-human learners)?
pred_justification: The paper states 5 test examples per concept per batch (120 = 8×3×5), and explicitly justifies this small size by "the limitations of conducting the experiments with humans" (line 219-220), without separately justifying why non-human learners (GPT-3, Louise, program induction) couldn't be tested on far more examples since they don't share humans' practical constraints; this is a legitimate, paper-grounded critique.

segment_text: Even after reading section 3 it was unclear to me how witness sets could be so small and what exactly the authors meant by priors being aligned between learner and teacher, and I was only able to understand what the authors intended by reading the Telle et al.
pred_justification: Section 3 presents the teaching-size/witness-set formalism (lines 141-172) largely through dense equations and abstract definitions with only one brief intuitive example ("considering two witness sets of the same teaching dimension, the example '(010101,1)' contains more information than '(0,1)'"), and the phrase "alignment of priors between learner and teacher" is introduced without much elaboration beyond citing Goodman and Frank (2016) and Yang and Shafto (2017). This is a plausible, specific clarity complaint grounded in the actual density of the section rather than a fabricated or out-of-scope claim.

segment_text: In particular, I think what I was missing was that witness sets only need to distinguish the shortest satisfying program from earlier, shorter ones.
pred_justification: The paper's teaching book definition (lines 161-168) matches this: it enumerates programs ordered by size and only includes a witness set/program pair if the program (shortest consistent one) hasn't appeared before, meaning witness sets need only distinguish the target program from earlier, shorter ones already covered in the book — consistent with the reviewer's stated understanding.

segment_text: Most of the paper is pretty clear, although I had trouble understanding section 3.
pred_justification: The segment is a subjective, unspecific comment ("had trouble understanding section 3") without identifying what specifically was unclear in the theoretical framework section (teaching size, prior alignment), making it hard to verify or act on, though Section 3 is indeed dense with formal notation.

segment_text: It is very possible that some of the empirical findings are specific to quirks in these 8 concepts.
pred_justification: The paper's experiments are built on a fixed set of 8 abstract concepts (referenced repeatedly, e.g. "8 × 3 explanations", "the 8 concepts" line 229); flagging that findings might be idiosyncratic to this small, fixed concept set is a reasonable generalizability concern not contradicted by the text.

segment_text: I would suggest keeping the current setup for the human comparisons, but greatly expanding the number of programs for the automated systems (much more than in the supplementary material).
pred_justification: The paper itself states (Discussion, line ~362): "the use of humans for comparisons limits the number of concepts and test examples that we can do for a reasonable questionnaire, and more concepts were tried only for GPT-3 (see supplementary material)." This confirms the exact asymmetry the reviewer describes and supports the suggestion to expand automated-system testing while keeping the human setup as is.

segment_text: In addition to the mathematical definitions, I would appreciate if the authors could explain more thoroughly in plain text.
pred_justification: Section 3 (lines 145-168) presents the teaching size, program capture, and teaching book definitions in dense formal/mathematical notation with only sparse intuitive explanation (e.g., a single odd-number analogy), so a reasonable reader could find the plain-text exposition thin; this is a specific, grounded readability critique rather than a vague or unsupported one.

segment_text: I would say upfront that I am not an expert in this topic, and have found many points in the paper unclear, perhaps due to this.
pred_justification: The segment is a generic self-disclaimer ("not an expert," "found many points unclear") without identifying any specific unclear point in the paper, so it cannot be checked against the text and matches the Vague Critique pattern seen in examples like "Some parts about the proposed method are not clear" without further specification.

segment_text: Methodologically, I'm a little concerned that the experiments don't fully address what the authors are after.
pred_justification: The segment gives no concrete detail about which experiments or research questions are inadequately addressed; the paper explicitly lays out six research questions (Q1-Q6) and answers each in the Discussion section, so a specific gap would need to be named to be actionable.

segment_text: From the definition of "capturing a concept" in #154 we have "iff for every S we have that p 􏰑 S iff c 􏰑 S.".
pred_justification: The paper (lines 152-154) states verbatim: "A program p captures concept c iff for every S we have that p ⊨ S iff c ⊨ S," matching the segment's quoted definition accurately.

segment_text: In particular, it seems like what we'd really like to know is what concepts the learner has learned, but instead we measure accuracy.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly attempts to go beyond accuracy by eliciting explanations of the learned concepts (Q6, Section 5, lines 305-315, 353-357), even if this effort was only partially successful for GPT-3 ("we did not get good explanations consistently"). The segment implies the paper only measures accuracy and never tries to probe what concepts were learned, which overlooks this explicit explanation-based analysis.

segment_text: In what sense does accuracy improve once you've captured a concept?
pred_justification: The paper explicitly frames this as Q2 ("Does accuracy increase from the theoretically minimal witness sets needed for teaching the concept with additional examples?") and answers it directly, showing learning curves where "the accuracy increases as additional examples are provided (AS I and AS II)" and explaining that the minimal set is "rarely sufficient" because system priors are not perfectly aligned with the simplicity prior. The reviewer's question overlooks this explicit discussion.

segment_text: In particular, the paper uses "fairness" without clearly explaining how fairness is measured.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly defines its fairness notion throughout: individual fairness measured via invariance of classifier predictions to counterfactual sensitive-attribute perturbations, formalized as similarity specifications and validated via a crowdsourcing study (abstract: "classifiers must be fair... by being invariant to perturbations of sensitive attributes such as gender or ethnicity"). The claim that fairness measurement is left unexplained overlooks this explicit definition.

segment_text: The fairness metric used seemed a bit ad hoc.
pred_justification: The segment gives no specifics about what makes the metric "ad hoc," while the paper extensively justifies its learned similarity metric (crowdsourced validation, active learning, relabeling, Balanced Accuracy evaluation, Table 3), so this generic label is unsupported and non-actionable.

segment_text: However, it is hard to understand the experiment sections without referring to the appendix in detail.
pred_justification: Section 4 repeatedly defers key details to appendices (e.g., "Implementation details are described in App. B", "See App. C for more details", "Further details can be found in App. D", "More detailed experiments... can be found in App. B and D", extended Tables D.1/D.2/D.4), so the criticism that the experiments section is hard to follow without the appendix has real support. However, this is somewhat subjective/mild (a common pattern in ICLR papers with appendices) and lacks specific identification of which parts are unclear, keeping it from being a fully specific, high-confidence critique.

segment_text: For example, in Table 2, the authors do not provide any description of the "Metric/Method" column in the main text.
pred_justification: The paper text uses the phrase "Metric/Method group transfer" without ever formally defining "Metric/Method" as a labeled category in the main text (line 53); its meaning must be inferred from context and the appendix survey questions, so the reviewer's complaint about missing description has some basis, though the term's meaning is reasonably inferable.

segment_text: I had a hard time processing the multitude of experimental results. In particular, it's not clear what the numbers represent in each table.
pred_justification: The segment gives no specifics on which table or numbers are confusing, and the paper explicitly explains Table 1's contents ("numbers in italics" = matched constraint set performance, "numbers in bold" = generalization performance, with balanced accuracy and fairness criteria labeled), contradicting the vague claim that it's unclear what the numbers represent.

segment_text: I would clearly describe in the caption of each figure what the rows/columns represent and what metric is used.
pred_justification: The paper's tables (e.g., Table 1, Table 2) do lack fully self-contained captions describing rows/columns/metrics directly in the caption itself (details are scattered in body text like "in Table 1" descriptions), so there is some basis, but the segment is a generic, non-specific formatting suggestion that could apply to almost any paper and doesn't identify which specific figure/table caption is problematic.

segment_text: Similar problems happen in Table 3.
pred_justification: The segment merely asserts "similar problems happen in Table 3" without specifying what the problem is, referencing an unspecified prior complaint; Table 3 (active learning classifier results in Sec 4.4) is presented with clear methodology and caveats already discussed by the authors (relabeling, threshold tradeoffs), so without a concrete stated issue this reads as an unsupported, non-specific critique.

segment_text: Not clear what WR50 means.
pred_justification: The term "WR50" does not appear verbatim anywhere in the paper text; the paper discusses "word replacement" (WR) and mentions "the 50 identity terms from Garg et al. (2019)" separately, but table/notation like "WR50" (likely referring to a table column or word-list size) is not clearly defined in the visible text, e.g. Table D.1's "Censoring Both WR" content is garbled/truncated in extraction, making it plausible the term is genuinely underexplained, though this could also be an extraction artifact rather than a real omission.

segment_text: Last but not least, I think "fairness specifications" is misleading and quite an overblown term for what the paper is about;
pred_justification: The paper grounds "individual fairness specifications" precisely in the established individual fairness framework (citing Dwork et al. 2012, Kusner et al. 2017) and consistently uses the term to mean formal similarity specifications for downstream classifier training, so the reviewer's claim that the term is "misleading" and "overblown" is an unsupported subjective opinion rather than a substantiated critique.

segment_text: A better word choice might be something like "coverage".
pred_justification: The segment is a bare one-line word-choice suggestion with no indication of which term in the paper it targets (e.g., "diversity" is used throughout Sec 4.2/4.3 to describe the constraint set), so it cannot be checked against the paper text and reads as an unsubstantiated stylistic nitpick rather than a grounded critique.

segment_text: The word choice of "diversity" sounds strange, given the evaluation criterion.
pred_justification: The paper operationalizes "diversity" via a classifier's ability to distinguish word-replacement pairs from style-transfer/GPT-3 pairs (91.6% accuracy) and via cross-evaluation of fairness constraint sets, not a direct semantic/linguistic diversity metric; questioning whether "diversity" is the right word for this evaluation criterion is a specific, paper-grounded terminology critique rather than vague or unsupported.

segment_text: For weaknesses, the authors could be clearer on what fairness metric is being used for tables such as Table D.3.
pred_justification: The paper does describe the metric loosely as "fraction of fairness constraints according to φ adhered to" and accuracy near the D.2/D.3 caption text, so the metric isn't fully undefined, but the caption itself is dense and the reviewer doesn't specify what exactly is unclear about it, making the critique only partially grounded and somewhat vague/non-specific.

segment_text: I find the MTPB dataset to be largely uninteresting, as it relies on very fine-grained natural language supervision. It's not clear to me whether it adds value over the Django dataset of Oda et al.
pred_justification: The paper never mentions the Django dataset (Oda et al.) at all, and explicitly motivates MTPB as filling a gap since it is "the first multi-turn program synthesis benchmark" (paper text near line 13), so the reviewer's comparison and dismissal ("largely uninteresting") is an unsupported claim not grounded in any paper passage discussing Django.

segment_text: CodeGen model (single-turn) is only evaluated on a single dataset with only 164 problems. Why is the model not evaluated on other publicly available coding datasets such as MBPP and APPS?
pred_justification: The paper's single-turn evaluation (Section 3) indeed only uses HumanEval's 164 problems and does not report results on MBPP or APPS, so the factual claim is accurate; however this is a fairly generic "why not more benchmarks" critique common to many code-generation papers, slightly weakening its specificity.

segment_text: Novelty is limited since there are already several pre-training/dataset collection papers in this area.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly acknowledges prior pre-training/dataset-collection works (CuBERT, CodeBERT, PyMT5, CodeT5, Chen et al. 2021, Austin et al. 2021, Li et al. 2022) and frames its novelty not as pre-training/dataset collection but as the multi-turn program synthesis paradigm and the new MTPB benchmark ("we contribute... a novel multi-turn programming benchmark"), so the segment's generic novelty critique misconstrues where the paper claims its contribution lies.

segment_text: It is unclear why Table 2 only has information about CodeGen-Mono and not the other models. More data here would be more convincing.
pred_justification: The paper states Table 2 reports perplexity of pass vs non-pass problem prompts "based on samples from CODEGEN-MONO models," a specific analysis designed to test whether prompt perplexity predicts synthesis success for that model family, not a general model-comparison table that omitted other models.

segment_text: The result will stand out to compare against Codex, the state-of-the-art program synthesis model.
pred_justification: The paper already performs a direct, detailed comparison against Codex in Table 1 and the surrounding text ("Our Python-monolingual CodeGen models have competitive or improved performance, compared to the current state-of-the-art models, Codex... CODEGEN-MONO 16.1B is competitive or outperforms it depending on k"), so the segment's implication that this comparison is notably absent or noteworthy as a gap overlooks content explicitly stated in the paper.

segment_text: The MTPB dataset contribution needs more explanation regarding its practical use cases and its limited capability to handle more complex programs.
pred_justification: The paper already gives extensive explanation of MTPB's construction, purpose (measuring multi-step program synthesis capacity), and problem categories including complexity levels (easy/medium/hard, Section on difficulty analysis, Figure 2), so the claim that it "needs more explanation" is vague and unsupported by specific gaps; the "limited capability to handle more complex programs" point is also not tied to any concrete evidence from the text.

segment_text: (-) MTPB (from a cursory qualitative evaluation of examples) seems to rely on very fine-grained prompts. In many examples in App F, the prompts are substantially longer than the required code.
pred_justification: The paper's MTPB is explicitly designed as a multi-turn factorization benchmark (Section 3.1) where prompts are deliberately decomposed into fine-grained natural-language steps to study intent understanding; critiquing prompt length relative to code length is beyond the paper's stated scope, matching the annotated Out-of-scope example for this exact segment.

segment_text: My main concern with this approach is that the paper does not discuss how to apply this approach to more general problems.
pred_justification: The Discussion section explicitly addresses this: "The current limitation of RoT is the need for supervision to learn divide and conquer for each task. In order to apply RoT to a wider range of tasks, it may be crucial to reduce the expensive supervision," and further discusses generalization limits and future architectures. The paper does discuss applying the approach to more general problems and its limitations, so the reviewer's claim of an absent discussion is not supported.

segment_text: The formulation doesn't scale to general reasoning problems, the tasks considered aren't tasks that you would train a specific LM to solve, and the algorithmic solution is very simple/trivial extension.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly targets narrow, well-known formal tasks (arithmetic and classic DP algorithms like LCS/LPS/knapsack/MCM) using teacher-provided recursive procedures "borrowed from elementary school math" and "standard, well-known algorithms" (Sec 3.3/4.1) rather than claiming to solve general reasoning, and the Discussion section already acknowledges the need for task-specific supervision as a limitation, so the "doesn't scale to general reasoning" point largely restates an acknowledged, in-scope limitation. Calling the recursive divide-and-conquer contribution (special GO/STOP/THINK/TAIL tokens enabling recursive multi-context inference, Algorithm 1) a "trivial extension" is an unsubstantiated, subjective dismissal similar to the guideline's "straightforward/not surprising" Invalid Criticism examples, since simplicity/being a natural extension of CoT is not in itself a demonstrated flaw.

segment_text: As a result, outside of tasks such as arithmetic operations where the dataset can be created automatically (and one could argue that you wouldn't use a task specific LM as the paper doesn't deal with multiple tasks or out-of-distribution problems), the applicability of this approach is minimal.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly demonstrates RoT not just on arithmetic but also on four algorithmic tasks (LCS, LPS, 0-1 Knapsack, MCM), all with automatically generated ground-truth via teacher programs (Section 3.3, 4.1, Appendix D), contradicting the segment's framing that applicability is minimal "outside of tasks such as arithmetic operations." While the paper does acknowledge a genuine limitation (need for task-specific supervision, Section 5), the segment overstates this by implying only arithmetic-like automatically-generated-dataset tasks work, neglecting the algorithmic task results already reported.

segment_text: On the negative side, the solution proposed is formulated as a fully supervised problem, meaning for each task the exact steps needed to solve the problem needs to be annotated.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly states RoT is trained "in a supervised manner" where "we assume that ground truths for the intermediate steps of how to recurse are readily available" (Sec 3.1), and the Discussion section explicitly names this as a limitation: "The current limitation of RoT is the need for supervision to learn divide and conquer for each task." The segment accurately reflects this stated limitation.

segment_text: This is not a scalable approach as for realistic real-world applications obtaining detailed annotations for reasoning problems is an expert task which is expensive to scale to large datasets.
pred_justification: The paper's own Discussion section explicitly concedes this limitation: "The current limitation of RoT is the need for supervision to learn divide and conquer for each task. In order to apply RoT to a wider range of tasks, it may be crucial to reduce the expensive supervision." This directly supports the reviewer's scalability concern, though the paper frames the ground-truth generation as automated teacher programs for the tested arithmetic/algorithmic tasks rather than strictly "expert annotation," so the "expert task" framing is a slight extrapolation beyond what's stated.

segment_text: Unfortunately, I don't see much impact from this work in practical terms.
pred_justification: The segment gives no specifics about what "practical impact" would look like or why the demonstrated results (GPT-3 achieving near-perfect accuracy on extremely long arithmetic/algorithmic reasoning problems that were previously unsolved, Section 4.2) fail to matter; it is a generic, unsubstantiated dismissal rather than a grounded critique tied to paper content.

segment_text: So, in its current form this does not enable any new abilities as we could use the base algorithm instead of using expensive LMs.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly states its purpose is to test whether language models can learn to reason/generalize underlying rules via divide-and-conquer under context limits ("we evaluate whether a model understands the underlying rules, instead of brute force memorization"), not to provide a practically useful replacement for a deterministic arithmetic algorithm; dismissing the contribution because "the base algorithm" could be used instead trivializes the research question the paper is actually investigating.

segment_text: In terms of the insight from a learning point-of-view, I also do not see anything surprising in this work.
pred_justification: This is a purely subjective "not surprising" judgment with no supporting argument, similar to guideline examples where such vague "unsurprising" claims are deemed invalid criticism; the paper's RoT mechanism (recursive multi-context divide-and-conquer via special GO/THINK/STOP/TAIL tokens enabling tiny 536K-parameter models to solve tens-of-thousands-of-token reasoning problems, Sections 3 and 4.3) is presented as a genuinely novel paradigm, and the reviewer gives no basis for dismissing its insight value.

segment_text: The novelty is minimal as the solution proposed is rather trivial as it doesn't try to solve the hard problem of reasoning without direct supervision, or other settings such as few-shot/zero-shot/multi-task and formulates the problem as a fully supervised task.
pred_justification: The paper does explicitly say RoT is supervised (§5: "current limitation of RoT is the need for supervision to learn divide and conquer for each task") and does not target few-shot/zero-shot settings, but the reviewer's characterization of the contribution as "rather trivial" is an unsupported subjective judgment that ignores the paper's actual technical contributions (special tokens GO/STOP/THINK/TAIL, recursive context management, tail recursion, and the demonstrated ability to let tiny randomly-initialized models solve extremely long-horizon reasoning tasks that CoT cannot handle within the context limit), similar to the "results not surprising"-style Invalid Criticism examples in the guideline.

segment_text: So the high accuracy of the resulting method is not that surprising.
pred_justification: This is a subjective, unsubstantiated dismissal similar to guideline examples like "Results are not particularly surprising" which are explicitly marked unreliable; the paper explains RoT's high accuracy comes from reducing each context to a simple base-case problem via recursive divide-and-conquer (Sections 3.1-3.3), a specific mechanistic explanation the reviewer doesn't engage with, and the paper frames the near-perfect accuracy as a substantive finding (e.g., enabling tiny 536K-parameter Transformers to solve 32-digit multiplication) rather than an obvious result.

segment_text: Therefore, it would be great if the authors could explain the limitation of the problems that RoT could solve and how to design proper subproblems in order to use RoT to train the models.
pred_justification: Section 5 (Discussion) explicitly states limitations of RoT ("The current limitation of RoT is the need for supervision to learn divide and conquer for each task", and that "RoT cannot facilitate length generalization"), and Section 3.3 explicitly describes the desiderata for designing subproblems/reasoning procedures ("each context should be short, and the next tokens to generate should be obvious from the previous sequence"). The reviewer's request for this information overlooks content already present in the paper.

segment_text: However, the technique only seems to work for problems for which we already have algorithms, and it is unclear to me if this could be extended to more general problems.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly relies on hand-designed teacher programs based on known algorithms (elementary-school arithmetic procedures, DP algorithms) to generate supervision, and the Discussion section admits: "The current limitation of RoT is the need for supervision to learn divide and conquer for each task. In order to apply RoT to a wider range of tasks, it may be crucial to reduce the expensive supervision." This directly corroborates the reviewer's concern about extending the technique beyond problems with known algorithms.

segment_text: The problems considered here are very simple, and an algorithm to solve them needs to be known in order to generate the training data.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly confirms this: Section 3.3 states "we design an exemplary reasoning procedure for each problem type and implement it as a teacher program that automatically generates the contexts given a problem," and that arithmetic procedures are "borrowed from elementary school math" while algorithmic tasks use "standard, well-known algorithms." The authors themselves acknowledge in Section 5 (Discussion) that "the current limitation of RoT is the need for supervision to learn divide and conquer for each task," directly corroborating the reviewer's claim that a known algorithm is required to generate training data.

segment_text: My main concern is on how to properly train the RoT framework as the training of RoT requires (non-trivial) human inputs to design proper subproblems.
pred_justification: The paper's Discussion section explicitly states: "The current limitation of RoT is the need for supervision to learn divide and conquer for each task. In order to apply RoT to a wider range of tasks, it may be crucial to reduce the expensive supervision." This confirms training RoT requires designing exemplary reasoning procedures/subproblems by hand (as also described in Section 3.3, "we design an exemplary reasoning procedure for each problem type"), which directly supports the reviewer's concern about non-trivial human input.

segment_text: After decomposing the problem manually (i.e. by writing an algorithm to generate training data), the learning task is pretty simple (for addition, for example, all the model has to do is to extract the last digit from two numbers).
pred_justification: The paper explicitly confirms this: RoT's training data is built by "a teacher program that automatically generates the contexts" (§3.3), and the base-case addition subproblem in the worked example (Fig. 1 / Appendix A) is literally single-digit addition of the last digits (e.g. "8+1=9"), matching the reviewer's claim that decomposition reduces the learning task to something trivial like extracting/adding last digits.

segment_text: [-] The training of RoT requires (non-trivial) human inputs to design proper subproblems.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly acknowledges this in the Discussion section: "The current limitation of RoT is the need for supervision to learn divide and conquer for each task," and Section 3.3 confirms that a "teacher program" and "exemplary reasoning procedure" must be manually designed for each problem type (e.g., borrowing elementary school arithmetic procedures). This directly supports the reviewer's claim of non-trivial human input for designing subproblems.

segment_text: My main concern is on how to properly train the RoT framework as it requires people to feed it with hand-designed subproblems.
pred_justification: The paper itself acknowledges this exact concern: Section 3.3 states RoT requires ground-truth intermediate steps built from "an exemplary reasoning procedure for each problem type" (hand-designed teacher programs), and the Discussion section explicitly names "the need for supervision to learn divide and conquer for each task" as "the current limitation of RoT."

segment_text: One important point missing from this work is how to systematically construct subproblems given any problem in order to teach the model learn the recursion of thoughts.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly concedes in §5 Discussion: "The current limitation of RoT is the need for supervision to learn divide and conquer for each task. In order to apply RoT to a wider range of tasks, it may be crucial to reduce the expensive supervision," and §3.3 confirms the recursive procedures are hand-designed "exemplary reasoning procedures" per task type (borrowed from elementary school math or standard algorithms), not a systematic/general construction method for arbitrary problems. This matches the segment's claim almost verbatim, so it is well-grounded rather than a misunderstanding or neglect.

segment_text: The baseline WebChild in Table 2 seems to extract a much higher number of tuples at 4.6M, while the proposed model ROBERTANET only extract 6741 tuples.
pred_justification: The paper's Table 2 caption/discussion (line 41) explicitly notes "The acceptance rate...in Table 2 are not comparable to each other, and only serves for a rough sense," and frames the comparison around precision/accuracy rather than tuple count, arguing their setting trades quantity for accuracy without training data. The segment's raw factual observation about tuple counts may be accurate but ignores the authors' explicit framing that scale is not the intended comparison axis, making it a partially valid but incomplete critique.

segment_text: It can be WebChild having much higher coverage, but this difference was not discussed in the paper.
pred_justification: The paper cites WebChild only as one of several related text-mining extraction systems (line 17) and never compares coverage/scale against it directly in any experiment or table, unlike COMET and LPAQA which are used as explicit baselines; so the claim that a WebChild coverage comparison/discussion is missing is factually accurate, though whether this omission is a meaningful weakness (WebChild targets a different, narrower relation set) is debatable.

segment_text: This, in my opinion, is not reasonable because it would result in a sparse KG.
pred_justification: The segment is a bare reviewer opinion ("not reasonable... would result in a sparse KG") without specifying what proposal or threshold it is reacting to, and the paper text (Section on scoring thresholds, e.g. base-10/base-100/50% settings) already discusses multiple thresholding strategies for controlling KG density/scale, so the claim is not clearly grounded in a specific paper passage nor explained.

segment_text: The effectiveness is not significant compared with SOTA baselines.
pred_justification: The paper states their approach "substantially outperforms other baselines, like COMET on ConceptNet and LPAQA on LAMA" and shows significant accuracy improvements (e.g., Top-1 Prompt improves up to 9% over Human Prompt, Multi-Prompts adds another ~4%), contradicting the claim that effectiveness gains over SOTA are insignificant.

segment_text: The experiment is not comprehensive.
pred_justification: The segment gives no specifics about which experiments, datasets, or comparisons are missing; the paper actually reports extensive evaluations (link prediction, human evaluation of precision/diversity/novelty, ablations across multiple LMs like BERT and RoBERTa, and comparisons to prior KG construction/completion methods), so the bare claim "not comprehensive" is an unsupported, generic critique.

segment_text: The methodological novelty of the paper is fairly low.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly frames its contribution as empirical/scaling (EXMIX task collection + extensive study of transfer, §1, §2) rather than a novel architecture; EXT5 itself is "a T5 model pre-trained on a mixture" (§1), so the paper is largely upfront that novelty lies in scale/analysis, not a new method, making a bare "low methodological novelty" claim a subjective, under-justified critique similar to the Invalid Criticism examples about straightforwardness/novelty not being independently reliable.

segment_text: The paper completely reuses the T5 strategy for multi-task learning and just scales it up with more tasks.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly studies EXT5, which combines self-supervised span denoising with supervised multi-task pre-training on the newly introduced ExMix (107 tasks) and performs systematic analysis of co-training transfer among task families, not merely reuse of T5's strategy scaled up ("we propose EXT5... pre-trained using a multi-task objective of self-supervised span denoising and supervised ExMix"). The segment ignores this added supervised+self-supervised combination and the transfer analysis as the paper's core contribution.

segment_text: The scientific value of this work predominantly comes from the scale of their multi-task setting, and their analyses.
pred_justification: The paper's abstract explicitly presents EXT5 (a new multi-task pre-training objective combining self-supervised span denoising and supervised ExMix) as a core contribution with concrete gains on SuperGLUE, GEM, Rainbow, and Closed-Book QA, not merely scale and analysis; the segment trivializes this modeling contribution similarly to the "results are not surprising"/"straightforward" pattern flagged as Invalid Criticism.

segment_text: While this scaling could have been an interesting study, the ablations and empirical investigation don’t ask very interesting questions for this to be useful. I didn't find any significant recommendations for scaling tasks that can be reusable in future work or even applicable to models other than T5. Moreover, prior work (Aghajanyan et al., 2021) also studied most of these questions already, in the context of two pre-trained models, though in a slightly different setting. Over this and much other related work on multi-task and multi-lingual learning, the current paper only seems to contribute new results using the T5 model.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly distinguishes itself from Aghajanyan et al. (2021), noting it has "approximately twice as many tasks" and studies "multi-task pre-training rather than fine-tuning" (unlike Aghajanyan's pre-finetuning setup), and the paper provides concrete actionable findings (e.g., large batch sizes are essential for task scaling to help, §2.5; multi-task pre-training beats pre-finetuning, §2.3), so the claim that it merely rehashes prior work with no reusable recommendations trivializes documented contributions.

segment_text: Many of the results presented in motivating the work are over random subsets of pre-training tasks and random seeds for training. However, none of the results seem to give an idea of the variance of performance, nor any indication of how many different random subsets of tasks were used for the results.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly states "We repeat this over three random seeds, and report average scores in Figure 4" (line 37), so the number of seeds is in fact stated, contradicting the reviewer's claim that there's "no indication of how many random subsets/seeds were used"; however, it is true no variance/error bars are reported, only averages, so the core variance concern is partially valid.

segment_text: The task scaling experiment (2.5) seems to be core to the contribution of the paper. Similar scaling experiments are also present in Aghajanyan et al., (2021). However, apart from the lack of an exposition of the variance in the quantities presented, I found this analysis to be very underwhelming.
pred_justification: Section 2.5 states they "repeat this over three random seeds, and report average scores in Figure 4" but the text gives no variance/spread/error-bar information for these averages, supporting the reviewer's specific claim about lack of variance exposition; the broader characterization of the analysis as "underwhelming" is a subjective add-on but the core factual claim is grounded in the paper.

segment_text: However, the models use the same R parameter across numbers of tasks, which seems unfair to low-task settings given that it was tuned on 107 tasks.
pred_justification: The paper states in §2.4 that R=2 "worked best for our BASE-sized models" and then reuses this same R=2 across the 30/55/80-task scaling experiments (§2.5) without re-tuning per task-count setting, supporting the reviewer's concern that a single R tuned in one context is applied uniformly across different task-count regimes.

segment_text: There are some details missing regarding Section 2.4, especially with respect to random seeds.
pred_justification: Section 2.4 explicitly states "We repeat this over three random seeds, and report average scores in Figure 4," directly addressing random seeds, so the claim that seed details are missing overlooks this stated detail.

segment_text: However, I am concerned that this will be used as a point of reference to say that randomly adding more tasks always helps, for which the paper doesn't provide sufficient evidence.
pred_justification: Section 2.5 explicitly reports task-scaling experiments (30/55/80 tasks, three random seeds, base model) showing that "increasing the number of tasks being mixed generally helps downstream performance" with large batches, which is direct evidence for the claim the segment says is unsupported; the reviewer's concern about generalizability of this claim is reasonable but the specific assertion that "the paper doesn't provide sufficient evidence" understates the controlled experiment the paper does present.

segment_text: Additionally, the models use the same learning rate regardless of batch-size, ostensibly a learning rate that was tuned for a batch-size of 512.
pred_justification: The paper (section on scaling number of tasks) states models are trained "with batch sizes of 128 and 512" but never states the learning rate is fixed across both batch sizes or that it was tuned specifically for batch-size 512; the reviewer's specific claim about learning rate being untuned for smaller batch sizes is not supported by any explicit statement in the text.

segment_text: Section 2.5 uses the same learning rate for different batch sizes, which might result in unfair comparison given there are previous works suggesting how batch size, learning rate could have compound effects on the downstream tasks.
pred_justification: Section 2.5 (line 37) states models are trained "with batch sizes of 128 and 512" using the same pre-training setup/learning rate schedule described elsewhere, with no mention of adjusting learning rate for the different batch sizes, so the reviewer's concern about a potential confound between batch size and learning rate is grounded in the text.

segment_text: Section 2.5 compares different numbers of tasks trained on different batch-sizes.
pred_justification: Section 2.5 ("Does Adding More Tasks Help? Task Scaling Experiments") explicitly trains models with batch sizes of 128 and 512 and compares 30, 55, and 80 tasks, matching the segment's description exactly.

segment_text: In section 2.4, will R beyond 10 still lead to consistent improvement of the SuperGLUE performance is unclear.
pred_justification: Section 2.4 (paper_59.txt line 33) only reports that R=0 hurts performance and that R=2 "worked best," referring readers to Figure 3 without stating the full range of R tested in text; the paper gives no textual evidence about behavior at R>10, so the reviewer's question about unclear behavior beyond R=10 is not contradicted by the text and could be a legitimate gap, though it is not fully verifiable without seeing Figure 3 itself.

segment_text: Overall the idea of this work is novel, but the description is very hard to follow.
pred_justification: The Thrust method description (e.g. the dense derivation around lines 21-25 involving t_v, t_b, weighted unit vectors and cluster distances) is admittedly technical and could plausibly be hard to follow, but the segment gives no specifics about which parts are unclear, making it a vague, unsubstantiated critique typical of the "Vague Critique" pattern.

segment_text: Clarity: some important terms are not defined at all or until later in the paper, including the key term of external knowledge (which commonly means something else actually, as in knowledge graphs).
pred_justification: The paper defines "external knowledge" starting in the abstract and introduction (line 9, 13) and explicitly enumerates its sources (knowledge graphs, Wikipedia paragraphs, human annotations) in Section 3.2 (line 33) and related work (line 57), directly overlooking the reviewer's claim that the term is undefined or defined only late in the paper.

segment_text: The methods (and experiments) are described informally, or obscurely, where the specific choices made are not motivated or compared to alternatives.
pred_justification: The paper does motivate its design choices (e.g., Section 2.1 explains the Thrust metric's derivation, cites Murty et al. 2021 for the binary thrust variant, and gives intuitive justification via the cluster-distance framing), so the blanket claim that "specific choices made are not motivated" is not well supported; the segment also fails to specify which particular methods/experiments are "informal or obscure," making it a vague, generic critique rather than a grounded one.

segment_text: There are some typos and style issues.
pred_justification: The segment claims typos/style issues exist but gives no examples or specifics; a search of the paper text found no clear evidence of such issues, and the claim is too vague to verify or act on, matching the Vague Critique pattern (cf. Example 6/28 in the guideline about unspecified typos/missing details).

segment_text: However, one might wonder why only the result of UnifiedQA is shown?
pred_justification: The paper explicitly states in the Thrust evaluation section, "we evaluate the effectiveness of Thrust with the UnifiedQA models" and explains this is because "a pre-condition of Thrust is that the external knowledge is useful," which UnifiedQA (transfer-learning) models satisfy; Table 2 also reports T5 and OPT results in addition to UnifiedQA, so the claim that only UnifiedQA results are shown overlooks both this justification and the broader model comparisons already present.

segment_text: why not also compare to the case using knowledge 100% of the time?
pred_justification: The paper already reports the 100%-knowledge case in Section on cost-efficiency: "We denote simply using external knowledge for all instances as a costly but straightforward way... Table 4 presents the comparison between adaptive and indiscriminate knowledge propulsion" and notes "for the e-SNLI, Web Questions, and NQ, the full knowledge setting performs better than Thrust." The reviewer overlooked this explicit comparison.

segment_text: The experiment result also need more explanations.
pred_justification: The segment gives no specifics about which experimental results need explanation, while the paper actually provides detailed discussion of results in paragraphs 37, 41, 45, and 53 (e.g., analysis of ARC-C failure cases, layer-wise ablations, and reasoning for Table 2-4 trends), making this an unsupported generic critique.

segment_text: Comparing the results in Table 2 and 3, on many of the tasks, using Thrust to partially utilize the external knowledge drops the performance compared to when all queries are answered with external knowledge (e.g., 70.2 → 56.8 (75% of queries) on e-SNLI UnifiedQA-base, 80 → 73.4% (75% of queries) for TriviaQA UnifiedQA-3b).
pred_justification: The paper itself explicitly discusses this exact phenomenon in the Table 4 analysis: "for the e-SNLI, Web Questions, and NQ, the full knowledge setting performs better than Thrust" when only a partial fraction of instances get knowledge, attributing it to the manually-written, high-quality nature of e-SNLI's external knowledge. The reviewer's qualitative claim (partial-knowledge Thrust underperforms full-knowledge on tasks like e-SNLI/TriviaQA) is directly grounded in the paper's own reported finding, though the exact numeric values (70.2→56.8, 80→73.4) could not be independently verified against the extracted table text.

segment_text: This paper is very unclear.
pred_justification: The segment "This paper is very unclear" provides no specific details about what is unclear, matching the Vague Critique pattern where the review lacks specificity about missing or problematic components.

segment_text: The experiments miss some important baselines.
pred_justification: The segment does not specify which baselines are missing; the paper already compares Thrust against random sampling and full/no-knowledge settings (Table 4, Section on effectiveness), and discusses related hardness/confidence estimation methods (RDA, V-Usable Information, Sensitivity Measurement) as prior work not directly comparable since they require test labels, so the critique lacks the specificity needed to be actionable.

segment_text: Table 2, if my understanding is correct, with knowledge case is presented after the vertical bar (|).
pred_justification: This is merely a hedged clarifying question about table formatting ("if my understanding is correct"), not a substantive critique pointing to any actual flaw in the paper; the table itself isn't reproduced in the extracted text to even confirm or refute the claim, making it an unsupported, non-actionable comment.

segment_text: If that's true, please fix the description of the model which states the opposite.
pred_justification: The segment is a conditional fragment ("If that's true...") that doesn't specify what claim is being verified or which part of the model description supposedly states "the opposite," so it cannot be checked against the paper text (e.g., Section 2.1's IAPEK/Thrust description) and reads as an unspecific critique.

segment_text: Such an important typo makes the paper difficult to understand.
pred_justification: The segment claims an "important typo" makes the paper hard to understand but does not identify what the typo is, and no such typo issue is discernible in the paper text, matching the Vague Critique pattern of unspecific missing/erroneous components.

segment_text: Some experimental setup details are missing, making the results difficult to be reproduced for now.
pred_justification: The paper does leave some details underspecified (e.g., |C| the number of K-means clusters is only vaguely stated as "relative to the size of estimated instances" rather than a concrete number), but the segment itself never identifies which experimental setup details are missing, making it an unspecific, unfalsifiable critique per the Vague Critique pattern.

segment_text: For example, the authors did not indicate the number of clusters they used in the experiments, and how many knowledge instances they used to augment a query (which seems to be one).
pred_justification: The paper only says the number of clusters |C| "is relative to the size of estimated instances" without giving a concrete number used in experiments, and does not explicitly state how many knowledge instances are used to augment each query, supporting the reviewer's claim of missing implementation details.

segment_text: The authors only compare Thrust with random baseline, but in order to show the effectiveness of Thrust as a scoring metric, they should compare the algorithm with baselines simpler than Thrust but better than random, e.g., using BM25 scores.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly states "We compare the performance difference between Thrust and random sampling" (line 29) and Table 4 compares Thrust only against full/indiscriminate knowledge usage — no simpler-but-nontrivial scoring baseline (e.g., BM25-based) is used anywhere, confirming the segment's specific and accurate critique.

segment_text: While the motivation for identifying `hard cases' is 'limited bandwidth or budget to retrieve external knowledge', efficiency and computation time is not evaluated.
pred_justification: The paper motivates Thrust by "limited bandwidth or budget to retrieve external knowledge" (Sec 1/29) but only evaluates cost-efficiency indirectly through the fraction of instances (25%/50%/75%) sent for knowledge retrieval and resulting accuracy/F1; no wall-clock time, latency, or computation-time measurements are reported anywhere in the paper, so the segment's claim is accurate.

segment_text: The authors claim that they try to simulate the real-world case where they have limited bandwidth to retrieve external knowledge from the perspective of cost-efficiency, but the claim is not persuasive because the way they choose the portion of the queries to use external knowledge is through relative comparison between queries after scoring all other queries, and not through absolute scoring on each independent query, e.g., by applying a score threshold.
pred_justification: The paper confirms instances are selected via relative ranking/percentile of Thrust scores across the test set (Section 2.1: "we can set t as a particular percentile of S, e.g., top 25% of S") and evaluation uses fixed portions (25%/50%/75%) chosen by ranking rather than an absolute per-query threshold, matching the segment's claim.

segment_text: Few tasks here require complex reasoning, or deeper language understanding.
pred_justification: The paper's own description of its 24 instruction induction tasks (line 69) states they "span many facets of language understanding, from simple phrase structure to similarity and causality identification"—these are indeed largely simple pattern-matching tasks (pluralization, second letter, antonyms, rhymes) rather than complex reasoning benchmarks, so the segment's characterization is largely accurate, though the paper does include some causality/semantic tasks that could be argued to require some reasoning.

segment_text: Until then. it's unclear to me how this approach generalizes beyond simple tasks.
pred_justification: The paper's 24 evaluated tasks are mostly simple instruction-induction tasks (pluralization, antonyms, letter operations, etc.) plus TruthfulQA; it never tests APE on complex multi-step reasoning tasks (e.g., math word problems, logical reasoning), so the reviewer's concern about generalization beyond simple tasks is grounded in an actual gap, though the paper does include TruthfulQA (38 categories) which is somewhat more complex, keeping the criticism only partially strong.

segment_text: However, I'm not quite convinced if this approach can scale to more challenging NLP tasks.
pred_justification: The paper already evaluates on 24 diverse instruction-induction tasks plus TruthfulQA (health, law, politics, fiction), and explicitly discusses tasks that are "intrinsically challenging for the model" (e.g., Membership, Second Letter) where APE underperforms humans, so the segment's vague doubt about scaling to "more challenging tasks" doesn't specify what is missing given this existing coverage.

segment_text: Instead, most of the tasks can be solved with human-level accuracy using just the enumeration of a few input/output pairs as prompts (Fig. 4). These pairs would be available in any case since they are needed by the proposed method.
pred_justification: The paper states that in Figure 4, adding the APE-generated instruction on top of the raw in-context input/output pairs improves performance on 21 of 24 tasks over standard in-context learning alone, implying the plain enumeration of I/O pairs (without instruction) is generally worse, not already at human-level on "most tasks" as the segment claims; this contradicts rather than confirms the segment's characterization of Figure 4.

segment_text: Translation task is only done for single words. Semantic tasks from GLUE are at 90+% accuracy with simple transformer models.
pred_justification: The paper's instruction-induction tasks do include word-level translation (Translation en-de/es/fr) so that part is plausible, but the paper never reports specific per-task accuracy numbers in the text (only figures), so the claim that "semantic tasks from GLUE are at 90+% accuracy with simple transformer models" is not stated or supported anywhere in the paper text; it appears to be an unverifiable external claim not grounded in the paper's reported results.

segment_text: The idea of converting all the tasks to an unified format is not new, and has been explored in earlier works like DecaNLP, UFO-Entail, T5 and more recently in the CLUES few-shot benchmark.
pred_justification: The paper's own related work (line 17) acknowledges that unifying task formats is a known approach, citing McCann et al. 2018 (DecaNLP), Zhong et al. 2021 and Wang et al. 2021 (single-prompt/boolean-QA/NLI unification), and discusses T5's text-to-text format extensively as a basis for its method, confirming the reviewer's point that this idea predates the paper.

segment_text: For instance, the authors evaluate their models on held-out NLI tasks, but train their models on paraphrase identification tasks that bear some similarity with the entailment tasks.
pred_justification: The paper's Figure 2/training details confirm paraphrase identification datasets (MRPC, QQP, PAWS) are in the training mixture (line 97-101), while NLI is explicitly held out as a zero-shot task (line 21, 33). Since paraphrase identification and NLI both involve judging semantic relations between sentence pairs, the reviewer's concern about task similarity confounding the "zero-shot" claim is a specific, paper-grounded observation rather than a vague or unsupported critique.

segment_text: Can the authors report the multi-task model performance on NLI tasks without using the paraphrase identification tasks?
pred_justification: The paper trains on paraphrase identification tasks (QQP, MRPC, PAWS) and evaluates zero-shot generalization on NLI as a held-out task; its ablations (Section 6.2) only vary the number of prompts (p) and number of training datasets (d), not task-type composition, so there is no reported experiment isolating whether NLI generalization depends on structurally similar paraphrase-identification training data. This is a specific, paper-grounded, actionable question the paper does not address.

segment_text: Repeated experiments with different subsets of training/eval tasks can help shed some light as well.
pred_justification: The paper deliberately picks one fixed set of held-out tasks (NLI, coreference, story completion, WSD) with explicit reasoning for the choice (Section on task splitting), so while repeating with different subsets could add robustness evidence, the suggestion is a generic, non-specific ask that could apply to almost any multitask generalization paper rather than pointing to a concrete flaw in this paper's evaluation.

segment_text: However, we still rely on a vast amount of supervised data. In a way, the comparison with GPT-3 is not too fair.
pred_justification: The claim that T0 relies on supervised data is accurate, but the paper explicitly addresses the fairness of the GPT-3 comparison (excluding GPT-3's eval datasets from training, holding out entire task categories, verifying no data leakage, and even re-evaluating GPT-3 across multiple prompts via the API to compare robustness), which the reviewer's brief dismissal overlooks.

segment_text: Questions Can authors provide intuition about the performance of T0 vs FLAN on the datasets that T0 does better, or worse?
pred_justification: The paper already discusses this directly, stating "T0's performance is better than FLAN's on some datasets (CB, RTE, and Story Cloze) and worse on others (ANLI and HellaSwag)" and then offers several concrete hypotheses (multi-task vs single-task holdout, pretraining objective, prompt diversity, model scale) for the discrepancy, so the requested intuition is already provided.

segment_text: Do it mainly have to do with auto-regressive style versus encoder-decoder (that T0 does not predict the input)?
pred_justification: The paper explicitly notes in Section 5 that "Unlike decoder-only language models such as GPT-3, [T0] is not trained to generate the input" and in Section 7 lists encoder-decoder architecture (vs. FLAN's "standard autoregressive language models") as a key difference from concurrent work, so the reviewer's question about autoregressive vs. encoder-decoder as a driver of results is grounded in content the paper itself raises, making it a reasonable clarifying question rather than a misunderstanding.

segment_text: However, there are no comparison with auto-regressive model with the same pretraining and zero-shot task evaluation.
pred_justification: The paper extensively compares against autoregressive models for zero-shot evaluation (GPT-3 in Section 6.1, decoder-only BIG-Bench baselines, and FLAN in Section 7), and even explicitly discusses that its architecture/pretraining differs from GPT-3/FLAN as a confound; the reviewer's claim of "no comparison" overlooks these extensive comparisons, though the narrower point that no autoregressive model shares T0's exact pretraining is technically true and acknowledged by the authors themselves.

segment_text: What would also be interesting is to see/what's missing in the paper, is to carefully study the difference in domains of the training tasks, versus zero-shot evaluation tasks.
pred_justification: The paper already discusses this at length: it explains its task taxonomy construction (organizing by task format), explicitly reasons about why held-out tasks like NLI, coreference, and WSD are distinct from training tasks, and verifies in Appendix C that held-out task data is not leaked through pretraining. The segment's claim that this analysis is "missing" overlooks this existing discussion, though a more quantitative domain-similarity study is arguably still absent.

segment_text: In this setting, other tasks such as paraphrasing, QA, sentiment analysis, summarization, topic classification are not considered as zero-shot tasks, and only used for training, which makes an incomplete evaluation for zero-shot learning.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly and deliberately holds out NLI, coreference resolution, WSD, and story completion as the zero-shot evaluation tasks (Section 3), using paraphrasing, QA, sentiment analysis, summarization, and topic classification as training tasks by design, with clear justification (these are tasks humans generalize to naturally). This is an intentional, justified methodological choice, not an incomplete evaluation, so the criticism trivializes a deliberate design decision rather than pointing out a real flaw.

segment_text: This is important since it is often difficult to explicitly partition tasks into disjoint sets.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly states "Unfortunately, NLP task categorization is fuzzy, particularly if trying to isolate a unique skill" and that "grouping by task is an imperfect heuristic," directly supporting the segment's claim that disjoint task partitioning is difficult.

segment_text: The claim of "true" zero-shot generalization needs to be further supported by two more experiments as highlighted in the main review, namely, (i) analyzing the overlap in text from the MTL setup with that of the unseen tasks, and (ii) ablating paraphrase identification tasks to find the impact on NLI tasks.
pred_justification: The paper does check overlap between test-task text and the C4 pretraining corpus (Section on "Zero-shot performance estimation... searched for long common substrings"), but this is not the same as checking overlap between the MTL training task text and the held-out unseen tasks, nor does the paper ablate paraphrase identification tasks to isolate their contribution to NLI performance—both remain genuine, unaddressed gaps.

segment_text: The only evaluation on the size of multi-task training dataset is presented on BigBench dataset in Figure 5, which is different than FLAN zero-shot evaluation.
pred_justification: The paper contains a dedicated ablation on the effect of the number of training datasets (d) on the standard 11 held-out P3 tasks (paragraph starting "More datasets yield better median performance... Figure 7 shows that the median performance increases as the number of training datasets increases"), which is a controlled dataset-size evaluation independent of BigBench and directly comparable to FLAN's dataset-size ablation discussion. The segment's claim that the only dataset-size evaluation is on BigBench overlooks this Figure 7 ablation.

segment_text: Therefore I think it would make the paper much stronger if you were to show how that baseline performs on the tasks in Figure 5.
pred_justification: The paper text jumps from Figure 4 (main T0 vs baseline results) directly to Figure 6/7 (ablation on number of prompts/datasets); "Figure 5" is never referenced or discussed anywhere in the extracted body text, so I cannot verify what specific tasks or baseline comparison the reviewer is referring to, making the claim's specificity unconfirmable against the available paper text.

segment_text: However, the evaluated model (T0) is using pretrained weights of T5 for training, which implicitly learned multi-tasking during unsupervised pretraining of T5 model. This makes the evaluation biased and an unfair comparison to GPT3 model.
pred_justification: The paper's own intro explicitly notes that GPT-3 itself is hypothesized to acquire "implicit multitask learning" from its pretraining corpus (Section 1, citing Radford et al. 2019), so this property is not unique to T0/T5 and does not make the comparison to GPT-3 uniquely "unfair" as the segment claims. Additionally, the paper controls for train/test contamination via a dedicated pretraining-corpus overlap analysis (Appendix C), which the segment ignores.

segment_text: This contradicts the usual expectation about the EBP, namely that in the (M) case, the model would be "lost" in unknown territory and start to produce very poor text.
pred_justification: The paper explicitly reports this contradiction: in the shuffled/random prefix cases, "we still observe basic language structures in the sample," demonstrating a "self-recovery ability" that "can not be explained by exposure bias which claims that the errors along the generation process should, on the contrary, accumulate" (Section 3). The segment accurately paraphrases this finding.

segment_text: The main conclusion of the authors is that: "although the mismatch between the data and model prefix distribution exists, it is still in the model’s “comfortable zone”, and is not large enough induce drastic performance loss during generation".
pred_justification: The segment is an almost verbatim quote from the paper's own conclusion (line 61: "we hypothesize that although the mismatch between the data and model prefix distribution exists, it is still in the model's 'comfortable zone', and is not large enough induce drastic performance loss during generation"), also echoed in the abstract (line 9). The review accurately reports the authors' stated conclusion.

segment_text: But I would argue this is mostly an artifact of the experimental setup, as prefixing generation with D-string (of length L) only eliminates exposure bias up to position L, and then both evaluated systems (according to the generation process defined Section 4.1) use a standard auto-regressive LM generation process that makes them both subject to the exposure bias problem.
